1 
 
 REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change  deals with the 
action taken by  the Government on the recommendations/observations of the contained in its „Three 
Hundred Fifty Ninth Report‟ on „Demands for Grants (202 2-23) of the Department of Biotechnology‟. 
The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 15th March, 2022.  
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) 
in respect of all the seventeen recommendations/observations contained in the Three Hundred Fifty 
Ninth Report. The replies of the Department of Biotechnology have been categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 
Para Nos.:- 2.2, 2.4, 2.12, 3.6, 5.5 and 7.6 
  Total recommendations – 06 Accepted. 
  The Committee is pleased to note that the Department has accepted its six 
recommendations/observations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report. 
Chapter II:    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government’s replies:  
 Para Nos.:- 2.6, 2.13, 3.4, 5.4 and 5.6  
 Total recommendations – 05 Not to be pursued further.  
 The Committee is convinced with the explanations  furnished by the Department of 
Biotechnology and, therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations further. 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee: Para Nos.:- 3.8 
                           Total recommendations – 01 Not convincing reply. 
 The Committee is not convinced by the reply of the Department regarding the 
Recommendation conta ined in this Chapter and desires that the Department should 
furnish convincing action taken steps in respect of the recommendation. 
  
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government 
are still awaited- further recommendation: 
 Para Nos.:- 3.2, 3.3, 6.5, 6.6 and 6.7  
 Total recommendations – 05 To be pursued further 
 The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of the recommendations/observations made in Chapter 
IV of the Report. 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.  

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL REVIEW OF THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021-22 AND ALLOCATIONS MADE 
UNDER B.E. 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Committee notes that the Department has been allocated 13 per  cent less in B.E. 2022 -23 
as compared to R.E. 2021-22 and 26 pe.0r cent less in comparison to the B.E. 2021-22. The Committee 
also observes that the Department could not utilize its budget in the first two quarters of the year 2021-
22 owing to pandemic related restrictions imposed by the Ministry of Finance.                            
       (Para 2.2 of the 359th Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.2 The observation regarding lower allocation of BE 2022 -23 is noted. It is stated that the overall 
allocation was reduced by Ministry of Finance.  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3 The Committee notes, that the Department has been able to spend only about 65 per  cent of the 
R.E. allocation in 2021 -22 under the Central Sector Scheme „Biotechnology Research & 
Development‟. When compared with B.E. 2021 -22, this utilisation is even less, only about 58 per  cent. 
The Committee also notes that utilisation under the Central Sector Scheme “Industrial and 
Entrepreneurship Development” is 85 per cent.   The overall utilisation of R.E. 2021 -22 under the two 
Central Sector Schemes is about 72 per cent.                                                                     (Para 2.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.4 The Department noted the observation of the Committee. It is submitted for consideration of 
Committee that in FY 2021 -22 (up to March, 2022), the Department has spent 95.82% under 
“Biotechnology Research & Development”  and 99.49% unde r “Industrial and Entrepreneurship 
Development” with reference to R.E. of the Department. The overall utilization of R.E. 2021 -22 under 
the two Central Sector Schemes is 97.65%. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.5 The Committee recognises the need of an additio nal allocation of atleast Rs.500 crore to the 
Department of Biotechnology, in addition to the allocation made in B.E. 2022 -23 (Rs.2581.00 crore) . 
The Committee underlines the importance of the initiatives of the Department with respect to support 
to indig enous vaccine candidates under Mission COVID Surkasha and  timely completion of the 
projects and, therefore, recommends that the Department should seek additional funds from the 
Ministry of Finance at the supplementary/R.E. stage so that the Department is able to sustain its key 
programmes.                                                                                                                      (Para 2.12 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.6 The Department conveys sincere thanks to the Committee for considerin g the Department‟s 
request and recommending additional budget at the stage of R.E. Accordingly,  the Department will 
seek additional funds from the Ministry of Finance at the supplementary/R.E. stage. 
 
 
 

3 
 
HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT- INITIATIVES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Action Taken 
1.7 Department has planned to gradually increase the number of fellowship under DBT -Human 
Resource Development program specifically DBT -RA, DBT -JRF and DBT -Postgraduate Teaching 
Program. In 2022 -23, Department has increased the number o f fellowship under TATA innovation 
Fellowship and Janaki Ammal - National Women Bioscience Fellowship. Department has also started 
a new fellowship program -MK B han Young Researcher Fellowship with provision of 50 
fellowship/annum to retain the young and bright fellows holding PhD degree in areas of Biotechnology 
in the country. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.8 The Committee observes that while the participation under the various human resource 
development programmes is satisfactory in West Bengal, the numbers  of beneficiaries are miniscule in 
the other three States i.e. in Bihar, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. The Committee therefore, strongly 
recommends the Department to priorities its activities as much as possible, so that the under -served 
States/regions of th e country, which are lacking institutions supported by the Department of 
Biotechnology, can benefit more from the initiatives of the Department and can resolve the regional 
imbalances in the field of scientific research.                                                                    (Para 3.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.9 The Committee‟s s uggestion has been noted for timely action by the Department. Recently, 
Head, HRD Division of the Department of Biotechnology visited Patna , Bihar for creating awareness 
about Human Resource Development program of the Department amongst institutions located in Bihar 
State. Similar outreach workshops are planned to organize in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh for 
awareness of DBT Programs and activities in areas of Biotechnology. 
UMMID – UNIQUE METHODS OF MANAGEMENT OF INHERITED DISORDERS 
  Recommendation/Observation 
1.10 The Committee also observes that a p rogramme on Sickle Cell Anemia is also executed by the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and, therefore, recommend s the Department of 
Biotechnology to coordinate with the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research to ensure 
synergy of efforts and avoidance of duplicity.                                                                    (Para 5.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.11 The recommendation of the Committee is noted for compliance in future. 
BIOREMIDIATION – FUTURE OF INDIA’S WASTE MANAGEMENT  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.12 The Committee observes the efforts of the Department in promotion of research and 
development of technological platforms towards finding solutions for waste treatment. The Committee 
therefore recommends that the Department should promote its efforts in a holistic manner and involve 
other stakeholders as well so that the country can take lead in u sing cheap, effective and 
environmentally sustainable methods in dealing with the problem of waste treatment and management.  
                    (Para 7.6 ibid)  
Action Taken 
1.13 The suggestions/recommendations of the Committee have been noted and necess ary action will 
be taken accordingly. 
 

4 
 
 
CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE 
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLY 
OVERALL REVIEW OF THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021-22 AND ALLOCATIONS MADE 
UNDER B.E. 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1 The Committee takes note of the fact that particularly, budgetary reduction under the Head 
“Industrial and Entrepreneurship Development” is quite significant. It can be seen that the R.E 
allocation for the Scheme got reduced by 27 per  cent approximately in comparison to the B.E. 
allocation of the year 2021 -22.  Moreover, the current allocation made in B.E. 2022 -23  for the same 
has been reduced by 50 per cent in comparison to the already reduced R.E. allocation of 2021 -22. The 
Committee is at dismay as to how the Department of Biotechnology would be able to carry out its 
activities with such meager allocation. The Committee observes that since the Department has not 
been able to utilise the R.E. 2021 -22 allocations to its fullest, alloca tion in B.E. 2022 -23 have been 
reduced substantially. The Committee expresses its worry on this constant under -utilisation of funds 
especially under the Central Sector Scheme –„Biotechnology Research & Development‟ and strongly 
recommends the Department to ensure full utilisation of the funds allocated to it in B.E. 2022-23.    
                  (Para 2.6 of the 359th Report) 
Action Taken 
2.2 With regard to the observation of the Committee regarding the significant reduction of funds 
under the head “Industrial and Entrepreneurship Development”, the Department would like to bring to 
the notice of the Committee that in FY 2021 -22, the Department received an additional fund for 
supporting the „Mission Covid Suraksha‟, which is actually created the figurative di fference between 
the routine financial year Revised Estimate (R.E.) and Budget Estimate (B.E.).  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.3 The Committee further recommends that the Department should also explore for additional 
budgetary resources through internal budgetary reallocations.                                       (Para 2.13 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.4 The Committee‟s suggestion for exploring the additional budgetary resources through internal 
budgetary reallocations is appreciated . H owever, the Department of Bi otechnology being an 
administrative Department has no mechanism to generate the internal revenues except its autonomous 
institutions may generate a very small part of revenues through providing services or other means such 
as royalty, etc. 
HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT- INITIATIVES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.5 The Committee is constrained to observe that much of the physical targets for the year 2022 -23 
in respect of human resource development activities are similar in number, to those set  for 2021-22. 
While the Department is seeking a higher allocation for these activities, the Committee fails to 
understand why the targets are pretty much the same. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department to revise its physical targets for the y ear 2022-23, to a higher achievable number so that 
the benefits of the initiatives of Department can be made available to a larger section of the society. 
                               (Para 3.4 ibid)  

5 
 
    
UMMID – UNIQUE METHODS OF MANAGEMENT OF INHERITED DISORDERS 
  Recommendation/Observation 
2.6 The Committee expresses its deep dissatisfaction and discontent over the execution of 
programmes of the Department under UMMID initiative. It is agonizing to note that these 
programmes, though are well planned on  the paper, lack actual ground level execution. Identification 
of rare and genetic diseases has a far reaching consequence, not just to the patient and its family but 
also on the biotechnology and bio -pharmacology research and treatment infrastructure. The  
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Department to identify and resolve the lacunae in 
execution and speed up its efforts to achieve the set targets for the year 2021-22.          (Para 5.4 ibid)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
Action Taken 
2.7 Antenatal and newborn screening for genetic disorders, which account for up to 80% of the rare 
diseases, provides an opportunity for preventing disease occurrence or early management with positive 
outcomes.  Based on the above, the Department of Biotechnology has developed and implemented the 
UMMID initiative to address this major unmet need of India through establishment of NIDAN Kendras 
(genetic diagnostic centres), outreach for screening in aspiration al districts and training program for 
competence building in genetic diagnosis and counseling. This initiative, planned for long term 
sustainability, has secured a significant role in the National Policy for Rare Diseases 2021. 
2.8 Following due process of  financial and administrative approvals, the ground level 
implementation of the pilot phase of UMMID unfortunately coincided with the COVID -19 pandemic. 
The NIDAN Kendras were made fully functional even in the face of the resultant headwinds, including 
tying up of hospital resources for COVID management efforts. However, beneficiary turnout was 
highly reduced due to the pandemic and was insufficient to meet the screening targets. With the 
relaxation of COVID restrictions and following awareness campaigns by  the UMMID Centres, the 
rates of screening have started increasing. A 54% greater turnout for antenatal screening was seen in 
the 2nd half of the year 2021-22 compared to the 1st half. 
2.9 The establishment of new UMMID Centres under the phase II expansion  program has also been 
delayed due to the COVID pandemic. This is expected to be completed in FY2022 -23, and help to 
achieve the screening targets 
  Recommendation/Observation 
2.10 The Committee is also perturbed to see that the physical outreach of the three components under 
the UMMID initiative are limited to only few States of the Country. The Committee expresses its 
displeasure over this regional imbalance and recommends the Department to expedite its processes 
and engage with different stakeholders in other under-served regions as well. The Department should 
proactively reach out to District Medical Hospitals/tertiary care centre, partner with private 
hospitals/research institutes and support startups/pathologies in executing the vision of the 
Department under the UMMID initiative. The Committee also recommends that the Department should 
lay special emphasis on the North-Eastern Region and tribal belt of the country.            (Para 5.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.11 The ultimate target for UMMID program throu gh DBT efforts is to have at least one NIDAN 
Kendra in each state/UT, replete with all required infrastructure for a functional genetic lab, and with 
capacity to support a screening program at each aspirational district. 
2.12 The Department is implementing  Phase II of the UMMID Initiative under which around 40 
projects covering 53 components (28 NIDAN Kendras, 21 Outreach, 4 Training centres) have been 

6 
 
selected for funding. This will increase the number of NIDAN Kendras from 5 to 33, extending 
coverage to 21 states/UTs (58%). The number of aspirational districts under outreach will be increased 
from 9 to 30, spanning 18 states/UTs. The number of training centres will be increased from 6 to 10. 
The phase II expansion is expected to be completed within FY2022-23.

2.14 The Department is in agreement with the observation to reach out to various stakeholders,

HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT- INITIATIVES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.1 The Committee observes that the number of publications, patent s filed/granted and technologies 
developed/commercialized during 2021-22 are way less than the numbers achieved in during 2019 -20 
and 2020 -21. The Committee recommends that an updated data in this respect be provided to the 
Committee and the Department should take appropriate measures to collect data on real-time basis. 
                                                                                                                                           (Para 3.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
3.2 As per the recommendation of the Committee, an updated data regarding t he research outcome 
such as publications, patents, technologies is attached at Annexure-I. 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
3.3 The Committee vide para 3.8 of the 359 th Report had observed that the number of 
publications, patents filed/granted and techno logies developed/commercialised during 2021 -22 
were way less than the numbers achieved during 2019 -20 and 2020-21. The Committee finds that

THE GOVERNMENT ARE STILL AWAITED 
HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT- INITIATIVES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.1 On the basis of the information provided by the Department, the Committee observes that while 
the achievement of physical targets is satisfactory in case of providing s upport to post graduate 
teaching programmes and fellowship to Junior Researchers (DBT -JRF), the performance of the 
Department is unsatisfactory in awarding fellowships to research associates (DBT -RA). The 
Department has been able to provide Research associ ateship to only 38 candidates as against its set 
target of 100, for the year 2021-22.                                                             (Para 3.2 of the 359th Report) 
Action Taken 
4.2 Department has supported 178 ongoing Fellows and selected 38 new Fellows for award of DBT-
Research Associateship in 2021-22. A total of 1055 applications received in the year 2021-2022 for the 
award of DBT-Research Associateship. The Expert Committee for DBT-RA has made the selection of 
candidates based on the qualit y of proposal, Research & Development work done by candidate and 
presentation before the Committee. Department will advertise the scheme for 2022-23 and outreach the 
DBT-RA as well other Human Resource development programs in States from where less number of 
applications received or participations of less number of institutions. 
Further Recommendation/Observations 
4.3 The Committee notes the  interim reply and would like to be categorically informed about 
the details of States where less number of applicatio ns were received or participation of 
institutions were poor; when the scheme for 2022 -23 got finally advertised and finally the 
support for post graduate teaching programme and fellowship for Junior Researchers got 
disbursed in those States. 
HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT- INITIATIVES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.4  The Committee also observes that the reported number of fellows who got job placement is very 
low as compared to the total number of fellowships awarded under different categories. While this may 
be due to under-reporting and the fact that many fellows may not have apprised the Department about 
them getting a job placement, the Committee strongly recommends the Department to devise a 
mechanism of keeping the record updated in order  to enable a much better assessment of the outcomes 
and industry acceptance of the Department‟s fellowship programmes. In addition, the Committee 
recommends that the Department should form a high level research direction committee comprising of 
experts from academia and industry whose main purpose should be to steer the national research in 
biotechnology on a path which can translate into more employment as well as development of industry 
relevant products.                                                                                                               (Para 3.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.5 The Department has planned to organize  a job fair for students/fellows coming out from DBT -
HRD Programs for placement in industries.  Department has constituted  a high level Committee-DBT-
Steering Committee on Human Resource Development and Skill Vigyan Program. One of the terms of 
references of DBT Steering Committee is to advise on strategies for placement of students/fellows 
supported under DBT-HRD Scheme and Skill Vigyan program. 

9 
 
 
4.6 Department has planned to develop the online module for capturing the data of placement under 
various programs and report the same to Committee. 
Further Recommendation/Observations 
4.7  The Committee reiterates its recommendations as contained in para 3.3 and would like to 
be apprised about the progress made in this regard. 
SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMMES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.8 The Committee observes that while 57 projects for the year 2020 -21 of the Departme nt are 
underway/completed, no projects were initiated/setup in States like Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, 
Bihar, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Kerala. The Department also informed that the total cost of these 57 
projects is about Rs. 28 crore.                                                                                            (Para 6.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.9 The Biotechnology Based Program for Societal Development is a „National Level‟ program of 
Department of Biotechnology and proposals are invited against „Call for Proposals‟ from all parts of 
the Country. The proposals are screened and evaluated based on merit of Biotechnological intervention 
proposed and technical strength of the proposal in meeting the purpose of upliftment of backward and 
underprivileged sections of the Society.  
Further Recommendation/Observations 
4.10 The Committee notes that the reply is interim in nature and reiterates that the Department 
must take  necessary measures to ensure that the programmes/projects of the Department are 
evenly spread out and especially in the underserved regions. A detailed note in this regard may 
also be furnished to the Committee    
Recommendation/Observation 
4.11  The Committee is constrained to note that the initiatives of the Department are not evenly 
spread out across the country and are restricted to few States only. It is pertinent that the benefits of 
the societal development initiatives of the Department are purposefully implemented in the 
economically and socially backward regions. The Committee recom mends that the Department should 
evolve a more inclusive approach in selection of regions. Without the inclusion of those regions, which 
require scientific interventions and support as a stepping stone towards a path to prosperity and better 
life, the true aim of such societal development initiatives cannot be achieved.                  (Para 6.6 ibid)                        
Action Taken 
4.12 The Biotechnology Based Program for Societal Development is a „National Level‟ program of 
Department of Biotechnolog y and proposals are invited against „Call for Proposals‟ from all parts of 
the Country. The proposals are screened and evaluated based on merit of Biotechnological intervention 
proposed and technical strength of the proposal in meeting the purpose of uplif tment of backward and 
underprivileged sections of the Society. 
Further Recommendation/Observations 
4.13 The Committee notes the reply and wishes to be apprised about the specific measures 
taken by the Department towards inclusion of socially and economically backward regions.   
 Recommendation/Observation 
4.14 The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to evolve a policy of equitable 
distribution of resources/initiatives, so that the under -served regions of the country, which have till 

10 
 
date been, devoid of support from scientific institutions/initiatives of the Department of Biotechnology 
get the much needed push.                                                                                                   (Para 6.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.15 As per recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change, the Department will take necessary action for evolving a 
Policy on ensuring equitable distribution of resources across the country. 
Further Recommendation/Observations 
4.16 The reply of the Department is noted and the Committee wishes to be apprised in detail 
about the steps taken by the Department towards equitable distribution of resources across the 
country with special emphasis on under-served regions of the country.

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the action taken by  
the Government on the recommendations/observations of the contained in its „Three Hundred Sixtieth 
Report‟ on „Demands for Grants (202 2-23) of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research 
(DSIR)‟. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 15th 
March, 2022.  
2. Action Taken Note s (ATNs) ha ve been received from the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research‟ ( DSIR) in respect of  all the 21 recommendations/observations contained in the 
„Three Hundred Sixtieth Report‟. The replies of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research  
have been categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 
Para Nos. 2.6, 2.7, 2.8, 2.9, 3.4, 4.3, 6.5, 6.8, 6.10 and 6.18  
 Total recommendations – 10 Accepted 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Department has accepted its ten 
recommendations/observations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report. 
Chapter II:    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government’s replies: 
Para Nos. 5.4, 5.5, 5.6, 6.11, 6.9, 6.13, 6.14, 6.15, 6.16 and 7.10  
 Total recommendations – 10  Not to be pursued further 
The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Department of 
Scientific and Industrial Research  and, therefore, does not want to pursue the 
recommendations further. 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee: ‘Nil’ 
Chapter IV:   Recommendations/Observations in respe ct of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: Para No. 3.5 To be pursued further 
 Total recommendation- 01 
The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of recommendation/observation made in chapter IV of 
the Report. 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters. 

2 
 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
B.E. DEMANDED AND B.E. ALLOCATED FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022-23  
Recommendations/Observations  
1.1 The Committee recognises the need for an additional allocation of at  least Rs.100 crore to the 
Department, in addition to the allocation made in B.E. 2022 -23. The Committee underlines the 
importance of the timely c ompletion of projects and, therefore, recommends that the Department 
should review the capital requirements of the projects and explore internal budgetary reallocations to 
ensure availability of funds for the projects.                                                (Para 2.6 of the 360th Report)  
Action Taken 
1.2 Department thankfully acknowledges the Committee‟s recognition  towards need for an 
additional allocation of at least Rs. 100.0 crore in B.E. 2022-23. Department has noted the directions of 
the committee for compliance. 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.3 The Committee also recommends that, if required,  the Department should seek additional 
funds from the Ministry of Finance at the supplementary/R.E. stage so that the Department is able to 
sustain its key programmes; especially initiatives relating to research and development and Regional 
Transport Aircraft -SARAS.                                                                                                 (Para 2.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.4 As per recommendations of the Committee, if require d, Department will seek additional funds 
from the Ministry of Finance at the supplementary/R.E. stage to sustain its key programmes including 
initiatives relating to research and development and Regional Transport Aircraft – SARAS.   
Recommendations/Observations  
1.5 The Committee notes the initiative of the Department in raising funds through CSR donations 
and collaborating with other Departments/Ministries for sponsoring its projects and recommends that 
the Department should explore innovative ways of enhancing its outreach so that the capabilities of the 
Department in terms of research and development of technologies can be widely projected.  
                   (Para 2.8 ibid)                                           
Action Taken 
1.6 To receive and utilize CSR contributions from the corporates, CSIR has developed Policy and 
Guidelines for proper and effective utilization of CSR funds available with the corporates. Subsequent 
to issuance of CSIR Guidelines, Ministry  of Corporate Affairs has issued amendment through 
notifications and clarifications with regard to Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 which have been 
endorsed to be followed by CSIR Labs over and above CSIR Guidelines. 
1.7 During Covid-19 pandemic, CSIR through its labs has  been continuously exploring availability 
of CSR funds with Industries/ corporates for establishing Covid -19 testing facilities, Make Shift 
Hospitals, Oxygen Enrichment Units and Face Masks. CSIR labs will make further efforts to tap CSR 
funds available with Industries/ corporates and utilize them for the benefit of the society.  
 
 

3 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.8 The Committee notes that the Department had demanded Rs. 12.93 crore in B.E. 2022 -23 
towards assistance to CEL, a PSE of the Department, but no funds have been allocated for the same. 
The Committee recommends that the Department should seek funds at the R.E. stage and also explore 
other avenues of re-appropriation of funds towards CEL, if such need arises.                 (Para 2.9- ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.9 Department will follow the recommendations of the Committee. 
ADDITIONAL BUDGETARY REQUIREMENT FOR DEVELOPMENT OF CIVILIAN 
AIRCRAFT-'SARAS' BY CSIR-     NAL 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.10 The Committee accordingly recomme nds that the Department should be given an additional 
fund of at least Rs. 95.06 crore so as to ensure that activities relating to development of SARAS are 
completed without any further delay.                                                                                 (Para 3.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.11 Department acknowledge s with thanks for the said recommendation and its support for the 
project.  It may kindly be noted that SARAS Mk2 project activities have picked up and pre -CDR 
review of major sub sys tems like Landing Gear, Wheels and Brakes, Flaps, Airframe structures were 
completed by January 2022. During the FY 2022 -23 it is planned to initiate the design and fabrication 
of Jigs, fixtures and tooling and procurement of LRUs initiated during the year  2021-22.  Hence, the 
minimum anticipated requirement for smooth execution of the SARAS project is Rs. 95.06 crores. 
DEPARTMENT’S INITIATIVES ON DRUG DISCOVERY FOR MALARIA 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.12      The Committee is cognizant of the fact that since malaria is a disease common to the entire 
country, especially in the densely populated pockets, low cost and effective treatment is absolutely 
essential to save poor pepole’s life, loss of productive man hours and decrease the need for 
hospitalisation. In this backdrop, the Committee applauds the efforts of the Department in research 
and development of drugs for the treatment of malaria. The Committee observes that all scientific 
advancements serve their purpose only when those are implemented in the welfare of the larger 
populace and, therefore, recommends that the Department should initiate a programme on a mission 
mode, along with other stakeholder Departments/Ministries, with a target of reaching out to a sizeable 
population in the most affected ar eas and create awareness about the various interventions of the 
Department in treatment of Malaria.                                                                                  (Para 4.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.13 Department thankfully acknowledges the Co mmittee‟s recognition for the  Department‟s efforts 
in research and development of drugs for the treatment of malaria.   
1.14 The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP), part of the Technical 
Division of the Directorate General of Health S ervices, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare is 
proactively involved in attending the directions mentioned towards programme on Malaria along with 
other stakeholder Departments/Ministries. 
1.15 CSIR thorough its constituent laboratory Central Drug Research  Institute (CSIR -CDRI), 
Lucknow has a long -standing program on malaria drug discovery and development as well as parasite 
biology and drug target identification. CSIR-CDRI has been working on malaria parasite biology with  

4 
 
 
particular emphasis on identifyi ng new targets and pathways for designing novel interventions. Some 
of the notable achievements in terms of drugs and ongoing research programs are α, β -Arteether and 
elubaquine. Further, an anti -malarial late lead molecule, CDRI S011 -1793, is being develo ped under 
the CSIR IND mission. This antimalarial lead compound has shown excellent in vitro and in vivo 
potency against chloroquine resistant P. falciparum  strains as well as strains resistant to other anti -
malarial drugs. S011 -1793 has also shown efficac y in P. falciparum field isolates from Africa and P. 
falciparum and P. vivax field isolates from Brazil accessed through the Medicines for Malaria Venture 
(MMV). 
1.16    In addition to extramural projects addressing aspects of organelle biology, genome mai ntenance 
mechanisms, biochemical pathways and vaccine approaches, CSIR -CDRI also has a n ongoing project 
entitled “Chemical biology approaches towards dissecting non -canonical protein functions and novel 
targets in Malaria, Leishmania and Filaria parasites”. 
CSIR LABORATORIES 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.17 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department and recommends that under Phase II 
of the CSIR - Aroma Mission, where the Department targets to add an additional 30,000 hectares, 
special emphasi s should be given towards implementation of this programme in the aspirational 
districts. The Committee also recommends that mechanisms of ‘better price discovery’ be explored 
through enhanced marketing and value addition, so that farm incomes are further augmented.  
Further, providing technical and infrastructural support to farmers/growers will also help in 
generating employment in rural areas of the country.                                                        (Para 6.5ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.18 Department thankfully acknowledges the Committee‟s recognition and appreciation towards 
CSIR-Aroma Mission. 
1.19 The CSIR laboratories have collectively achieved considerable success in their efforts to bring 
about 30,000 ha of additional cultivated area under the CSIR-Aroma Mission Phase -II, and will 
hopefully meet the targets within the defined time period. Emphasis has already been given to include 
aspirational districts and other regions or districts which are frequently affected by the vagaries of 
weather like floods, cyclones and droughts. Furthermore, the unutilized fields are also being brought 
under cultivation by introducing some stress -tolerant crops. Even in areas where traditional crops are 
commonly affected by animal attacks, several aromatic crops have  been introduced that are not 
damaged by wild or domestic animals.  
1.20 A separate vertical for value -addition is part of the Aroma Mission programme, where 
technology related to value-addition is being developed so that the farmers' income could be incre ased. 
Efforts are also being made to connect the user industry with the farmers so that they may earn a fair 
price for their produce without having to go through a middleman. In addition, frequent meetings 
involving all the stakeholders including farmers, industry and scientists, are being arranged to examine 
and address the industry's needs as well as the difficulties faced by farmers. CSIR labs have been 
conducting frequent awareness or training programmes for the skilling of the farmers and to make them 
aware about the appropriate crop varieties and agro-technologies for maximizing their yields.  
1.21 In clusters where a large number of farmers are cultivating aroma crops, infrastructural support 
in the form of improved processing facilities has been prov ided to reduce post -harvest processing 
losses. Several Aroma Mission beneficiaries cultivating these crops have gone on to become successful 
entrepreneurs, making essential oil-based formulations or products and employing many others in rural 
areas. 
 

5 
 
 
CSIR-NGRI - Heli-borne survey technology for groundwater management 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.22 The Committee feels that the technological expertise of CSIR should be used to redress the 
challenges relating to sustainable management of underground water resources. The Committee, 
therefore recommends the Department to proactively reach out to State Governments as well as 
stakeholder Ministries/Departments at the centre and engage in mapping of underground water 
resources at a large scale.                                                                                                  (Para 6.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.23 The Department acknowledges with thanks the suggestions given by the Committee. Currently 
CSIR- National Geophysical Research Institute ( CSIR-NGRI), Hyderabad is closely working with 
Ministry of Jal Shakti, Central Ground Water Board and National Mission for Clean Ganga on issues 
related to mapping of groundwater resources at a large scale. The institute has already completed a 
pilot project in 5 states on the national aquifer mapping project of Ministry of Jal Shakti and Central 
Ground Water Board (CGWB) and is currently executing a project of ground water mapping and 
management in the arid regions of the country. Further CSIR-NGRI will conduct stake holder meetings 
with state government departments as well as Ministries/Departments in the near future on the 
heliborne geophysical investigations for groundwater exploration and management. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.24 The Committee observes th at as against a demand of Rs.5899.62 crore under the head ‘CSIR’ 
the Department has been allocated Rs. 5562.76 crore in B.E. 2022 -23, which is about Rs. 300 crore 
less. The Committee recommends the Department to raise internal budgetary resources and try t o 
offset the reduction in budgetary allocation and, if required, the Department should seek additional 
funds from the Ministry of Finance at the supplementary/R.E. stage so that the Department is able to 
sustain its key programmes.                                                                                              (Para 6.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.25 Department has noted the recommendations for   compliance.  Department will seek an 
additional fund from the Ministry of Finance at the supplementary/R. E. stage to sustain its key 
programmes/ projects.   
Recommendations/Observations 
1.26 The Committee further recommends that the Department should also constantly monitor the 
utilisation of funds under the various programmes on a quarterly basis and ensure optimal utilisation 
of funds.                                                                                                                             (Para 6.11 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.27 Constant monitoring is being made in CSIR for the utilisation of fu nds under the various 
programmes on a monthly/quarterly basis to ensure optimal utilisation of funds. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.28 The Committee is compelled to observe, that the number of patent applications filed and patents 
granted in India during the year 2021 -22 has been the lowest in the past five years.  The Committee 
strongly recommends the Department to give special emphasis in improving these numbers in the year 
2022-23.                                                                                                                             (Para 6.18 ibid) 
 
 

6 
 
 
Action Taken 
1.29 CSIR will follow the directions of the Committee and would encourage its constituent 
laboratories to improve its number of patent filings and grant in the year 2022 -23 based on commercial 
& Strategic interest of CSIR.  It would also conduct webinars/seminars/workshop to increase the IP 
awareness within its laboratories.

7 
 
 
CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE 
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLY 
 
SICKLE CELL ANAEMIA (SCA) MISSION 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.1  The Committee observes that the activities of SCA Mission remain confined to two states, i.e. 
Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra in the Phase I undertaken during the period from 2017-2020. The SCA 
Mission has now been extended to Madhya Pradesh in Phase II with plans to extend the same model to 
Jharkhand. The Committee also observes that a programme on SCA is also executed by the 
Department of Biotechnology and, th erefore, recommends the Department of Scientific and Industrial 
Research to coordinate with the Department of Biotechnology to ensure synergy of efforts and 
avoidance of duplicity.                                                                                                        (Para 5.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.2 Focussing on two states, Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh, CSIR SCA mission has developed a 
comprehensive screening model by taking a multi -pronged approach of population screening, 
especially focussing on school -going children, antenatal screening of pregnant women and new born 
screening. Close to 25 lakh children have been screened in the two states and patients and carriers have 
been provided support as mentioned above. Hundreds of target couples w ere identified and through 
prenatal diagnosis and counselling, birth of affected kids has been prevented. In our comprehensiv e 
mode, regular camps were conducted  in both states for a proper follow -up of the enrolled patients and 
designed a modified severi ty score which allowed patients to be categorized into mild, moderate and 
severe category and thus , enabled  the management  of disease . An interactive social communication 
network was established to address any social stigma, queries and confusion related t o SCA, 
management and prevention of disease. With the success of the model, the same has now been 
extended to certain regions of Madhya Pradesh and plans are in place  for covering the state of 
Jharkhand in near future. Early identification of  patients and carrier allows to conduct a targeted 
approach from the model that we have developed. CSIR is in discussion with DBT in dissemination of 
comprehensive model for management of SCA in the affected areas so as to increase the reach of 
screening, management and training of State health workers. 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.3 The Committee notes and appreciates the efforts of the Department towards early screening, 
treatment and management of Sickle Cell Anaemia. Since the disease is endemic to many tribal area s, 
cost effective and efficient scientific interventions are the need of the hour to prevent any further 
prevalence of this disease and improve the patient’s quality of life. The Committee, feels that 
identifying the carriers and avoidance of marriage of c arrier couples may -be successful in a limited 
manner to manage the disease. The Committee strongly recommends that appropriate interventions 
backed by effective policy/guidelines will go a long way in not only improving the quality of life of the 
SCA patients but also prevent and reduce the number of children born and affected by this disease. The 
Committee firmly recommends that the Department should engage with other national and 
international agencies undertaking research on gene therapy and gene editing  based treatment of 
Sickle Cell Anaemia.                                                                                                           (Para 5.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.4 Department thankfully acknowledges the Committee‟s recognition and appreciat ion towards 
early screening, treatment and management of Sickle Cell Anaemia.  
 

8 
 
 
2.5 The leads from the CSIR Sickle Cell Anaemia Mission on genome editing technology has been 
taken forward by CSIR -Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology ( CSIR-IGIB), New Delhi 
towards getting a multi -centric five year preclinical/clinical trial for ex vivo and in vivo gene editing 
approved by Department of Science and Technology (DST) in association with Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs. CSIR-IGIB will be undertaking the project in collaboration with few national and International 
organizations. The overarching goal of this proposal is the following: 
I. Evaluate cell therapy products (modified HSCs through endogenous CRISPR effectors) in 
appropriate DCGI/FDA recommended preclinical models; 
 
II. Identify, educate, counsel, and recruit potential participants of the trial using internationally 
accepted inclusion/exclusion criteria. Follow them before and after P1 CT for 24 months; 
 
 
III. Perform safety, toxicity and efficacy trials in preclinical settings; and  
 
IV. Clinical trial at Dept. of Haematology, AIIMS, New Delhi. 
Further, if required, engagement with international agencies will be done at a later stage. 
  Recommendations/Observations 
2.6 The Committee feels that the Department needs to take more proactive steps in increasing on -
ground presence and collaborate with local and State level stakeholders so that the solutions 
developed by the Department can actually reach to the affected masses and other intended 
stakeholders. To this effect, the Committee strongly recommends the Department to aggressively 
promote the use of Hydroxy urea therapy for the treatment of Sickle Cell Anaemia.      (Para 5.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.7 Other than the symptomatic treatment for SCA patients, hydroxyurea (HU)  is one of the 
cheapest and most commonly used alternatives for long -term management of such patients. It was 
earlier approved for use only in cancer in India and extended to Sickle Cell treatment. Although HU 
therapy provides a robust therapeutic response  in SCA patients, unavailability of various formulations 
in the absence of CDSCO approval has been a major reason for a poor compliance and hence 
variability in the response to HU therapy. Under the Mission, the CSIR - Indian Institute of Integrative 
Medicine (CSIR-IIIM), Jammu generated relevant information and data on its utility and in association 
with a private firm, which led to its approval from CDSCO/DCGI for its marketing for specific use in 
SCA children, post Phase-IV studies.

CSIR-NGRI - Heli-borne survey technology for groundwater management 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.8 The Committee feels that the technological expertise of CSIR should be used to redress the 
challenges relating to sustainable management of underground water r esources. The Committee, 
therefore recommends the Department to proactively reach out to State Governments as well as 
stakeholder Ministries/Departments at the centre and engage in mapping of underground water 
resources at a large scale.                                                                                     (Para 6.8 ibid) 
2.9 Further, the Committee recommends that this information should be made available to the 
public in a user friendly manner with special focus on promoting ground water recharge initiatives 
         (Para 6.9 ibid)

groundwater mapping, efforts will be made to communicate the recommendation of the committee to

CGWB and jointly work for developing a user friendly information system for the promotion of ground 
water recharge activities. 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.11 The Committee observes that in the year 2020 -21, against a target of 5000 fellowships, only 
2743 fellows hips were disbursed. The Department informed that due to COVID -19 pandemic, CSIR 
could conduct only one Joint CSIR-UGC JRF-NET exam and hence targets could not be achieved. The 
Committee further observes, that even-though only about 50 percent of the target set for 2020-21 could 
be achieved, the Department has completely utilised the budgetary allocation under the head for the 
same year.                                                                                                                          (Para 6.13 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.12 Department likes to inform that due to Covid19 pandemic the whole nation was affected and 
due to spread of virus and to save the lives of young researchers from catching virus, CSIR conducted 
only one NET exam and hence t he target envisaged could not be achieved during 2020 -21. It is also 
humbly informed that the total number of fellowship beneficiaries was about 8500 during the financial 
year 2020-21. The department utilized the complete budgetary allocation of Rs. 400 cr ore of 2020 -21 
for making payment of fellowship including pending stipend in respect of CSIR research fellows who 
were not paid earlier for various reasons including of not submitting their continuation reports or 
fellowship claim bills , etc. The expenditu re incurred during 2020 -21 also includes the expenditure 
incurred on other sub -schemes of the umbrella scheme “Capacity Building and Human Resource 
Development”.  Further, it is humbly apprised that the Demand for Grant during 2020 -21 for the 
scheme “Capacity Building and Human Resource Development” was Rs. 500 crore against which only 
Rs. 400 crore were allocated by the Ministry of Finance. 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.13 The Committee further observes with surprise, that the Department has substantially  reduced 
the targets for 2021 -22 by 60 percent, to only 2000 (as opposed to 5000 in 2020 -21) and yet the 
budgetary allocation under the head is higher for the year 2021 -22 as compared to 2020 -21 by 18 
percent (Rs. 75 crore). In addition to this counterintu itive allocation of funds, the Committee is very 
disturbed to note that so far no fellowships have been disbursed out of the target of 2000 for the year 
2021-22.                                                                                                                            (Para 6.14 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.14 Department likes to kindly submit that though in 2020, CSIR could conduct only one JRF -NET 
Exam but on the other hand due to the prevailing pandemic conditions across the country, CSIR 
extended the tenability of JRF-NET certificate (to avail the fellowship from CSIR) which is normally 2 
years from a particular date i.e. (a fellow has a time of 2 years of joining the fellowship after qualifying 
a particular JRF-NET Exam). For JRF-NET conducted in December 2017, June 2018, December 2018,

JRF-GATE or SPMF qualified candidate is eligible to get the fellowship for a period of five years from

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change  deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the contained in its 
„Three Hundred Sixty First  Report' on „Demands for Grants (202 2-23) of the Department  of 
Science and Technology‟. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok 
Sabha on the 15th March, 2022.  
2.  Action Taken Note s (ATNs) have  been received from Department of Science and 
Technology in respect of all the sixteenth recommendations/observations contained in the „Three 
Hundred Sixty First Report‟. The replies of the Department of Science and Technology  have been 
categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I:       Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
   Government:   
 Para Nos. 2.4, 2.11, 2.12, 4.5, 4.10 and 6.5  
             Total recommendations – 06 accepted  
The Committee is pleased to note that the Departme nt has accepted its six 
recommendations/observations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report.                            
Chapter II: Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to  
pursue in view of the Government’s replies: 
 Para Nos. 2.3, 2.5, 2.6, 4.9, 5.3 and 5.4  
           Total recommendations – 06 Not to be pursued further 
   The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Ministry and , 
therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations further.  
Chapter III:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee: Nil 
Chapter IV: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the  
Government are still awaited:     
Para Nos. 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, and 5.5 
           Total recommendations – 04 to be pursued further 
The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of  the recommendations/observations made by the 
Committee in Chapter IV of the Report.  
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.

Recommendations/Observations

Recommendations/Observations 
2.1 The Committee observes that the Department has been able to actually spend (till 
31.01.2022) ₹ 3624.87 crore, which is about 69 percent of R.E. 2021 -22 allocation and about 59 
percent of the B.E. 2021 -22 allocation.  Upon a deeper analysis, it can be seen that under the 
Head ‘Science and Engineering Research Board’ both the B.E. and R.E. alloc ation for 2021 -22 
was ₹900 crore against which the Department has been able to actually spend only Rs.523.96 
crore, which is about 58 percent of the R.E. allocation for 2021 -22 under that Head. Further, it 
can also be seen that the actual utilisation (till  31.01.2022) under the heads Science and 
Technology Institutional and Human Capacity Building and Innovation, Technology Development 
and Deployment has been only 52 percent and 60 percent of R.E. 2021-22, respectively.

Action Taken

Recommendations/Observations

‘Technology Development Board’ is Rs 100 crore which is about 33 percent higher as compared 
to R.E. 2021-22.                                                                                                 (Para 2.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.4 Under the head „National Mission on I nter Disciplinary Cyber Physical System‟  (NM-
ICPS), an amount of Rs 270.00 crore was  allocated in BE 2021 -22. As per the approved 
expenditure plan for NM -ICPS, an amount of Rs.123.66 crore was allocated for the Year -One 
(2019-20) and the same was released on March 27, 2020 i.e. at the end of the financial year, which 
was available for utilization during the next FY 2020 -21. Besides, an amount of Rs. 271.27 crore 
was allocated for the year 2020 -21 and almost the entire amount was released. Since, sufficient

impediment in implementation of the scheme. However, during the current fiscal 2022-23, an

SUPPORT TO STARTUPS UNDER NSTEDB AND TDB 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.8 The Committee is constrained to observe that while Rs.75 crore was allocated to the 
Department in R.E. 2021 -22 under TDB, it has been able to spend only Rs.23.04 crore, which is 
only about 30 percent. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that TDB should scale up 
its efforts to fully utilise the allocated funds and further take necessary steps so that maximum 
utilisation can be achieved for the year 2022 -23 as well. For this, the Committee recommends that 
the Department should enhance its outreach and promotional activities.              (Para 4.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.9 It may be noted that Technology Development Board  (TDB) is mandated to provide 
financial assistance in the form of loan or equity and/or in exceptional cases, grant to industrial 
concerns and other agencies attempting commercial  application of indigenous technology or 
adapting imported technology for wider domestic application. 
 
2.10 The financial assistance of TDB is released to borrower company in installments that are 
linked to associated milestones as per agreement executed w ith the industrial concern. Thus 
utilization of allocated funds is dependent on disbursement/s which may spread over project life 
cycle, however, demand of funds is always done at total TDBs commitment of the project/s.   
2.11 The Budget Estimate (BE) for FY 2021-22 was prepared based on the committed liabilities 
of previous year as on 31st March, 2021 and requirements of new project during Current Financial 
Year (CFY). The details of fund requirement and allotment for FY 2021-22 are as follows:- 
 
Budget Estimate: Rs 50 Crore 
Revised Estimate: Rs 155 Crore 
Fund Allocation: Rs. 125 Crore (Rs. 50 Crore received on 30.03.2022) 
2.12 The total committed liabilities as on 31.03.2021  However, due to multiple waves of this 
pandemic most of the ongoing projects were delayed and borrower companies could not achieve 
the targeted milestones as expected during FY 21-22. This resulted in   rescheduling / deferment of 
disbursements (cash outgo).  
 
2.13 Notwithstanding this pandemic, 06 new agreements have been signed with v arious 
industrial concerns in FY 2021 -22 with TDB‟s commitment Rs. 130.77 Cr ore. The first 
installments against these projects have already been released. Remaining shall be released when 
the associated milestones are achieved project wise.

2.14 Thus, i t can be seen that despite COVID 19 issues TDB could create new committed 
liabilities of Rs.130.72 Cr ore. The total committed liabilities as on 31.03.2022 is Rs.219 Cr ore as 
on 2022-23. 
 
2.15 Further, the Board, after joining of the new Secretary, has exte nsively enhanced its 
promotional and outreach activities. From Aug 2021 till date, the Board has participated in more 
than 20 outreach programs, in collaboration with various partners‟ organizations, industrial bodies 
/ educational institutes. The Board ha s also issued special calls seeking proposals in the sectors of

EXTRAMURAL RESEARCH SUPPORT PROVIDED BY THE DEPARTMENT 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.17 The Committee observes that in the States of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, 
Uttar Pradesh, Delhi and Tamil Nadu; the total number of projects fund ed by the Department in 
the years 2019 -20, 2020 -21 and 2021 -22 are 741, 812 and 591, respectively. The Committee 
further observes that the share of these six States in the number of total projects funded by the 
Department during these years is more than 50  per cent of the total projects funded by the 
Department in those years. Similarly, the amount of funding released to these States is more than 
50 per cent of the total funding released by the Department.                              (Para 5.3 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.18 The figures in the table referred are the details of year -wise funds received by the 
Academia/R&D institutions located within the jurisdiction of different states. Department of 
Science and Technology provides research and development grants p urely on competitive mode to 
the Institutions across the country. Proposals are invited from potential researchers/institutions 
across the country through open calls and the proposals received are evaluated based on their 
merits. Except for establishing th e State S&T Councils and the State Climate Change Cells, no 
other scheme/programme offers grants state -wise. It may be noted that ~50% of the S&T 
institutions (including ~25% of institutions of national importance and the Universities) in the 
country are l ocated in these five states, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, 
Delhi and Tamil Nadu have.  The higher ratio of S&T institutions along with the institutions of 
national importance are largely contributing to research & development activ ities and therefore, 
these five states are able to take away almost 50% of the total extra mural grant offered by DST.   
 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.19 The Committee is constrained to note that in the States of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, 
Jharkhand, Bihar and Rajasthan, the number of projects funded by the Department are 
approximately 11 per cent of the total projects sanctioned. The Committee is perturbed to observe 
that the efforts of the Department of Science and Technology are falling short in pro moting 
scientific research and technology development in the North-Eastern Region as well.  
              (Para 5.4 ibid)   
 
 

9 
 
 
Action Taken 
2.10 The States of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar and Rajasthan together 
accommodate to only ~7% of the total S&T institutions (including ~13% of institutions of national 
importance and ~13% of the Universities) of India. Further, the States in the NE region share only 
3% of the total S&T institutions in the country. Since, the extra -mural research grant offered to the 
institutions is through competitive mode at national level and the distribution of the institutions is 
not equitable among the states, State‟s with strong S&T institution -base are able to receive the 
majority of the EMR grant. Although D epartment of Science and Technology has been offering 
equal opportunities to all the researchers/institutions across the country, some of the 
researchers/institutions are able compete strongly to grab the EMR grant offered by Department of 
Science and Technology. Department of Science and Technology is well concerned about the 
difficulties and challenges of the NE region and have been putting concerted efforts through some 
of the programmes like Climate Change Programme, Science & Society Programme, State S&T 
Council programme, etc. to provide special attention for the researchers/institutions from the NE 
region.

NATIONAL MISSION ON INTERDISCIPLINARY CYBER PHYSICAL SYSTEMS (NM-
ICPS) 
Recommendations/Observations 
4.1  The Committee observes that National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber Physical System 
(NM-ICPS) is aimed at promoting development and translation of futuristic technologies 
especially in the areas of Artificial Intelligence, Quantum Computing, Machine Learning, 
Augmented reality, etc. These technologies are crucial to keep the country at the forefront of state -
of-the-art technology research. The Committee also recognizes that there is an immense scope for 
training of human resources and creating capabilities in these fields and make  them future-ready. 
The Committee thus is perturbed to note that the achievement of the physical targets under NM -
ICPS may get adversely affected due to shortage of funds.                                  (Para 3.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.2 Although the Mission started in 2018 after the approval of the Union Cabinet, it took some 
time to launch the Technology Innovation Hubs (TIHs). As a result, most of the TIHs have 
completed around one year of function till date. It is, therefore, stated that progress of the  TIHs 
may be taken as for a period of one year only. 
 
4.3 Due to the COVID -19 pandemic, the TIHs could not establish the required infrastructure 
and have faced challenges to recruit required manpower. Thus, the targets of the Job Creation, 
Skill Development and other parameters could not be met as per the Mission targets. 
 
4.4 A detailed review of the mission and all TIHs established under the same has been 
conducted through a National workshop on Technology Innovation in Cyber Physical Systems 
(TIPS) held on May 6-7, 2022 at IIT Madras, wherein all challenges and problem areas of the TIHs 
in achieving the physical targets have been identified. The Mission Office at DST is working 
towards addressing these challenges and finding solutions to them in a holistic way. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.5 The Committee is constrained to note that the  reply of the Department does not 
address the concerns of the Committee.  The Committee therefore desires that the 
Department apprises the Committee about the statu s of achievement of targets set for NM -
ICPS.

therefore recommends an additional allocation of Rs. 210 crore be given to th e Department at the

. REPORT 
1, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf. 
present the Thirty-seventh Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests for the year 1996-97 (Demand No. 22). 
2. In its meeting held on 8th and 22nd August, 1996 the Committee discussed in detail 
the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and Forests on the basis of 
documents made available and the submissions made before it by the Secretary and other 
officials of the Department. 
3. The Committee thanks the officers of the Ministry for replying to the clarifications 
sought by the Hon'ble Members and placing before it the required material to enable the 
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests . 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 9th 
September , 1996. 
5. India , the seventh largest country (area 329 million ha.) in the world, covers 2% of 
land area, while supporting 16% of human population (900 million) and 15% of cattle 
population (480 million): It is one of the 12 mega bio-diversity countries, commanding 7% 
of the world bio-diversity. India has merely 1% of forest area and 112% of grazing land of 
the world. Per capita forest area in the country works out to 0.08 ha. as against global 
average of about 1.00 ha. Forests in the country are thus subjected to enormous biotic 
pressures. 
6. The very existence of the country and its all-round progress is greatly dependent on 
sustainable development. lt is, therefore, vital 'that a check is exercised on the environment . 
Our hoary traditions of environmental conservation which have inculcated in us a deep 
reverence for nature and an awareness of the age-old truth that all forms of life, be it 
human, animal or plant are inter-woven and any damage to one may cause serious threat to 
the rest. The age-old traditions of environment protection and reverence to the mother 
nature have been given prominence in our national priorities. It is therefore duty of 
everyone of us to protect and improve the natural environment, including forest, lakes, 
rivers and wildlife and to have compassion for living creatures. However, it is being noticed 
that as a result of economic progress pressure is steadily increasing on the environment and 
the natural resources. 
7. Over the years , the countries have realised the importance of protecting environment 
and preserving forests for the welfare and good of the mankind . The organisation of the 
Stockholm Conference on Environment and Development in 1972 further provided impetus 
to this realisation amongst the countries, whether developed or developing. In India, the 
Departm ent of Environment, as a separate department, was set up towards the end of 1980. 
8. It is in our own intere st not to cause damage to the environment. Resour ces of the 
earth must bl! made use of in a sustainable manner. If we go on destroying natural 
resources , it would ultimately lead to our own extinction. There is no doubt that we must 
fecd anJ mcet the basic human needs of our population; but at the same time we have to 
n.:mcmbcr that our environment should not be damaged so much so that the existence of 
future generations of humanity is threatened.

9. Recorded forest area of the country is 77 million ha. (23% of country's geographical 
area) but actual tree cover is only 64 million ha. (19:47%) 'out of which 31 million ha. is 
degraded (25 million ha. between 0.1 to 0.4 density; 6 million ha. less than 0.1 density). 
Approximately, 70-75% of the country's rural population depends on forests directly. It may 
be relevant to mention that the tribal population increased during the last decade by 46.10% 
while forest cover decreased by 1930 sq. kms. Obviously, lesser forest area is catering to the 
needs of a larger population. As a result usufruct availability gets reduced leading to further 
degradation of forests. This creates a vicious cycle and the pinch is now being felt by rural 
poor including tribals. Marketing of non-timber forests produce (NTFP) has also added to 
the pressure on these resources. High population coupled with extreme poverty in rural 
areas has forced the people to borrow natural resources heavily against future (220 MT of 
fuelwood, 250 MT of fodder, 12 MT timber and countless NTFPs). In addition, the forests 
provide valuable environmental services which are difficult to quantify but of which we are 
all well aware. The very quality of life on this planet is directly dependent on a optimum 
forest cover which is well spread out throughout the country. It is estimated that at the 
market rate products worth Rs. 30,000 crores are drawn annually, primarily for subsistence 
uses from forest areas. However, funds available for forestry sector are around Rs. 1,000 
crores which is less than one percent of public sector outlay resulting in gross under 
investment. 
10. Forest Resource Assessment for the period 1980-1990 by the FAO has revealed 
that annual rate of deforestation in Asia and the Pacific is of the order of 1.0 million ha. 
whereas in Latin America and Africa it is around 6.0 million ha. and 3.0 million ha. 
respectively. However, forest cover of the country, which had been shrinking in the past has 
been largely arrested. State of Forest Report, 1993 published by Forest Survey of India 
reveals that forest cover of the country has increased marginally by 22 sq. kms. over the last 
assessment (1991). The Report further highlights the fact that forest cover in north-eastern 
region is falling alarmingly. As against overall increase in forest cov\!r by 1560 sq. kms 
(without interpretational corrections), forest cover in north-eastern region has declined by 635 
sq. km. bringing down the increase to 925 sq. kms. only. 
Functions of The Minis,ry 
11. The Ministry of Environment and Forests is the nodal agency in the administrative 
structure of the Central Government for the planning, promotion and coordination of 
environmental and forestry programme. Within the overall framework of its mandate, the 
main activities of the Ministry are conservation and survey of flora and fauna forests and 
wildlife, prevention and control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of degraded 
areas and protection of environment. These tasks are sought to be fulfilled through 
envirQ.nmental impact assessment; eco-generation; assistance to organisations implementing 
environmental and forestry programmes; enactment of environmental legislation; formu1a­
tion of environmental policies; promotion of environmental and forestry research, extension, 
education and training to augment the requisite man power; collection and dissemination of 
environmental information; international cooperation and creation of environmental aware­
ness among all sectors of the country's population. 
11.1 The Ministry has been made responsible for environment and ecology, including 
environment in coastal water, mangroves and coral reefs, excluding marine environment on

Himalayan Zoological Park; National assistance to Forestry Devdopment Sd1eme. 
11.2 There are number of factors contributing to the pollution prohh:m which has, of 
late, become very acute. One of the factors causing pollution is vehicular emission to the 
extent of 50 to 60 per cent of the air pollution in our nh:tro-citks. In Ddhi alone, it is 
estimated that the contribution will increase from (+l pc.r cl!nt to 72 per cent by the year 2000 
A.D. In order to contain the spread of air pollution. the Secretary of the Ministry in his oral

reduce the sulphur content. ,: ..

Forestry Research 
18. Since initiation of forestry research in India, valuable knowledge has been generated 
and documented as scientific finding on silviculture of over 550 species of trees; classification 
of forest types of India, Pakistan, Bhutan and Sikkim; European silviculture syst~ms 
embellished to suit tropical forests; successful introduction of exotics, Eucalyptus, Poplars, 
Tropical Pines, Acacias and Lucaena Leucocephala spp.; seed technology of over 80 
important forest tree seeds and management of bamboos etc. Over 2000 established sample 
plots have provided data for construction of yield and volume tables for over 120 tree 
species. The regime of preservation plots, established all over the country, since 1929, has 
helped in a better understanding of forest ecology, biodiversity and environment. In the field 
of utilisation of forest products, research has contributed valuably to the development of 
forest based industries in the country. The Arsenic-Copper chromate treatment for wood 
preservation development by the Forest Research Institute is now widely adopted through· 
out the world. Investigations on and documentation of mechanical and other properties of 
Indian timbers has helped industries utilising timbers. The Forest Research Institute also 
piom:crcd the process of pulping bamboos for paper making. 
19. Study and development of termite control measures; control of insect pests of Sal, 
Shisham, Teak and Babul rank among the foremost achievements in the entomology 
discipline. Similarly, many pioneering works were accomplished in the field of Forest 
mycology and pathology. Forest nurseries over the country have immensely benefited in 
producing quality seedlings using insect pest and disease control practices pioneered by the 
forestry researchers. Notable among achievements in Forest Genetics are the development of 
hybrids of Eucalyptus producing larger biomass creation of model seed orchards of teak and 
semul and tissue culture of eucalyptus. 
20. Researchers in Non-wood Forest produce (NWFP) have several important achieve­
ments of industrial importance to their credit, such as development of Rill method of

26. The Forest Conservation (Act), 1980 was enacted with a view to check indiscrimi­

make the system of feedback from field agencies full-proof, the Government should use the
