64. Control of pollution is one of the areas assigned to the Ministry. Here, the Ministry 
has sought total budgetary support of Rs. 73.48 crores of which Rs. 30.35 crores is on the 
plan side and Rs. 43.13 crores on the non-plan side. In 1995-96 the allocation on this head 
was Rs. 26.53 crores as per revised estimates whereas the actual expenditure was Rs. 10.98 
crores. In 1994-95 and earlier in 1993-94 the Ministry had sought Rs. 26.73 crores and 
Rs. 17.20 crores against the actual expenditure of Rs. 9.70 crores and Rs. 8.14 crores 
respectively. The Committee finds that the Ministry's record has persistently been that of non­
utilisation in the thrust areas of its assignments. Even though the first legislation on the 
control arad prevention of pollution was being considered by a Joint Committee of Parliament 
when the Stockholm conference on Environment and De\·elopment was held in 1972, the 
Committee observes that pollution has increased in alarming proportions be it the pollution of 
environment or that of water, and the impact thereof is being felt by one and all alike. The 
norms regarding discharge :of industrial effluents continue to be flouted and the control 
mechanism remaining only on paper. Even the drinking water being supplied by civic bodies 
in the country is not safe to drink. Chlorine content in the water is very high and in West 
Bengal detection of arsenic in the water supply in 630 blocks under 52 villages spread over 
7 districts has added to the gravity of the problem. 
As regards pollution, to cite an example, Delhi today is the fourth most polluted city in 
the world with 30% of its people suffering from respiratory disorders. About 2000 M'DD of 
pollutants are added to the city's air each day, out of which 64% is contributed by the two 
lakh odd vehicles mostly by two and three wheelers. Even the Government's move to 
introduce unleaded petrol is being thwarted by 81% petrol run vehicle owners. Many are even 
getting catalytic converters (cat con) removed. The reasons being the non-availability of 
unleaded petrol outside the metropolis. Secondly, for retrofitting a cat con a car bas to run on 
unleaded petrol without cat con for atleast 2000 Kms. While the car is being run without cat 
con on unleaded fuel, the ~mission levels are phenomenally high and far more hazardous than 
leaded petrol. 
65. The Co>mmittee therefore is of the view that it is time the Ministry seriously goes into 

the dimensions of the problem and educate Motorists as to the need to use unleaded petro l 
and other such products which result in a cleaner environment . 
The Committee is constrained to observe that the Ministry has not done anything 
significant to control the environmental pollution, the emphasis should be more on educative 
and preventive aspects than on punitive aspects. The whole approach needs to be radically 
altered and the utilisation of budgetary support should be oriented in thut direction only. 
66. Closely related to the ecology and environment are the grim revelations on the 
menace of carbon emissions threatening the globe with dire consequences. The carbon dioxide 
is the main "gree nhouse gas" responsible for the ea rth 's warming. Today, there is 30 per 
cent more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere than two centuries ago. Countries in Europe and 
North America produce more than half of the global carbon dioxide emissions e.g. North 
America produces 5.2 tonnes per head per hear, East Europe 3 tonnes, West Europe -2.1 
tonnes, China 0.6 tonnes, Africa 0.3 tonnes followed by India 0.2 tonnes. The global 
temperature has changed between 1870 and 1990; it has changed from minus 0.3 degree 
celsius in 1970 to plus 0.3 in 1990. One of the factors responsible for this is the record-level 
use of fossil fuels which boosts the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, which traps 
heat to increasing heights. Last year alone, carbon emissions from burning fossils and fuels all 
over the world reached 6.1 billion tonnes which marl<s an increase of one million tonnes over 
1991. The Committee has been given to understand that most Governments of industrialised 
countries are failing to meet the goal of limiting carbon set by the Framework Convention on 
climate change signed at the earth summit in 1992. The Committee is of the view that curbs 
on carbon emission are necessary. Even though the scientific concept of a friendly 
environment is relatively new to us something drastically needs to be done by the Ministry in 
this regard with a view to control the environmental pollution. 
The Committee has been given to understand that according to a WHO report released at 
the conference tropical diseases like malaria, dengue and cholera will rise sharply in Africa 
and Asia. Besides, malnutri ·tion and water scarcity will affect many more families ·. Changes in 
h)·drological cycle will alter rainfall patterns in many areas. Many inland areas in the tropics 
may insteud face droughts and drying up o'f rivers. According to a study 3 to 4 degrees 
warming may eliminate up to 85 of the remaining wetlands, wipling out many birds and turtle 
species. 
67. The Committee agrees tliat ther-e is thus an urgent need to bring about a consensus to 
finally reduce emissions by 50 to 70 per cent over the next few decades by taking steps to 
increase energy efticiency, limit carbon consumption and encourage transition to renewables . 
This is all the more necessary because scientific studies advocate a stabilisation target of 450 
PPI\1 by 2100 A.D., where eco-systems could naturally adapt to climate change . 
The Committee further agrees that access to emironment friendly technology and finance 
is critical for countries like China and India which are stated to be fourth and fifth largest 
producers of Green House Gases (GIIGs) respectively to curb their emissions. The Committee 
recommends that Government should join the attempts to activate the Global Environment 
Facility (GEF) , a multilateral fund set up by affluent nations to meet obligations under the 
UN climate ~hange convention and lend budgetary support. 
(>S. The Committee notes that the l\linistry 's record in utilisation of budgetary support on 
conservation programmes in the last two )'cars has been poor. In 1995-96, the Ministr y 
utilised Rs. 6.31 crores out of the budget prO\'ision of Rs. S uores which is about 80% . ln 
199-J-95 the l\linistry utilised Rs. -L56 crorcs out of a pro\i ~ i on of Rs. ~ cron:s i.e., 50.7%. 
The Committee observes that the l\linistry should widen its hori,_,nl and should concentrate on 

urgent areas of Consevation Programme. This would also ensure optimum utilisation of 
budgetary support. 
69. As regard the dependence of the country's rural population on forest resources the 
Committee's attention has been drawn to a su~:vey conducted by Self-employed Women's 
Association (SEW .t\) in some villages in Sabarkanth~ District in Gujarat where 93% of the 
families live below poverty-line. These women have to pay 200 to 300 per cent more than what 
paper mills pay for the same forest produce. Besides, the Adivasi women who are at best 
semi-literate and who tap gum are also required to obtain licence. Another agony of these 
women is that they are required to sell their produce to Government agencies at one-fourth of 
the ,market price. In the process when these women were operating 'illegally' they could earn 
Rs. 25'- per day but now as SEW A members when they wish to operat~ 'legally' they earn 
Rs. 121-per day with longer working hours and with the additional help of c,hildren who have 
to leave school to provide the necessary supportive labour. 
The Committee therefore, feels that a line has to be drawn on the exploitation of forest 
wealth by the tribal ' and rural population on the one hand and unauthorised exploitation for 
commercial purposes. 
70. Another important aspect related to the preservation of forests is the large scale 
devastation by fire. This aspect, the Committee feels, is being neglected due to lack of modern 
fire fighting systems and insufficient control, monitoring and communication system to contain 
and prevent such fires. 
71. This is one of the projects for which budget estimates for 1996-97 provide an amount 
of Rs. 44 crores. Already till 1995-96, an amount of Rs. 89 crores has been released to the 
ICEF by the Ministry. The objective or the ICEF is to enhance the capacity of Indian 
institutions and organisations to promote and deli~er sustainable development programmes. 
For this purpose the priority areas identified under ICEF are the following projects: 
(i) Enhancing the capacity : of Indian private and public sector institutions and 
organisations to undertake environmentally sustainable development and 
management of energy and water resources. 
(ii) Providing support for programms which specifically address the inter-relationship 
between poverty .and environmental degradation, especially as it affects women, in 
energy, land and water management activities at the community and village level. 
(iii) Providing support for public awareness of environmental issues, community 
participation and community-based management of energy, land and water 
resources. 
72. The Committee feels that there is no correlation between the goals set forth, the 
projects identified and the amount of funds provided to these projects. It is also not clear how 
the funds spent on these projects ultimately benefit women engaged h~ energy, land and water 
management activities at the community and village_ level and provide support for public 
awareness of environmental issues etc. Among the beneficiaries are certain institutions like 
M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation Project entitled "Coastal Wet Lands Mangrove 
Conservation and Management". The Committee is not aware whether there is any 
mechanism to monitor the satisfactory utilisation of funds by such beneficiaries. Further, 
certain amounts realised from the sale of commodities donated by the Canadian Government 
are also channelised to projects under ICEF. The Committee has not been apprised as to what 
are the commodities donated by the Canadian Government and how they are sold and the 
receipts accruing thereform are channelised to the project. Prima facie there seems to be a 

case for further investigation into the entire project and utilisation of the funds earmarked for 
the project. 
73. One of the projects under the head forestry is the Project Elephant for which the 
budgetary support amounted to Rs. 5 crores each year in the last three years namely 1993-94, 
1994-95, 1995-96. While the actual expenditure during 1993-94 was Rs. 5.69 crores, in 
1994-95, it went down to Rs. 4.80 crores and declined further to Rs. 3 •• 4 crore in 1995-96. 
The Committee was informed that the large portion of the funds were provided to the State of 
Kerala for providing an 'Elephant Corridor' in ldukki and Parambikulam. The amount was 
disbursed to the State Government through District Collector and so far about 60 hectares of 
land had been taken over by the Ministry for the establishment of corridor in Kerala. The 
Committee was also informed that they have planted trees on an area of 400 acres of land. 
While the total budgetary provision for the project is Rs. 23 crores of which the corridor will 
require roughly an amount of Rs. 4 crores 25 per cent of the amount is to be spent on 
strengthening of infrastructure namely specialy wireless stations as elephant is considered to 
be a wide ranging animal. Asked about the details of the project and the number of trees etc. 
planted all these years in the elephant corridor, the Ministry could not furnish details. 
Besides, it was stated that a census was conducted for estimation of elephant population by 
direct count and index count in different parts of the country during 1992 and 1993. The 
habitat restoration and improvement activities have resulted in reduction of the period of 
man-elephant encounters thus mitigating the man-elephant conflict in such areas. 
74. The Committee is not happy with the progress made by the Ministry in the Project 
Elephant. Despite whatever has been done by the Ministry, one elephant is killed everyday. 
The generation of elephants appears to have completely stopped. There are no details 
provided by the Government indicating whether life of any elephant has been saved anywhere 
as a result of large amounts spent by them under the scheme. The Committee feels that the 
figures furnished by the Government regarding increase in the population of elephants from 
23,000 in 1989 to 25,000 in 1993 are not realistic. On the other hand, a large number of 
elephants die for reasons other than poaching. The Committee recommends that tliis project 
should be closely monitored and detailed notes on action taken with results, indigenous species 
planted with survival rate, number of wireless sets given, etc. should be furnished to the 
Committee. 
. 
75. The Animal Welfare Board has been provided with budgetary support of Rs. 1.64 
crores in the budget estimates for 1996-97 of which Rs. 1.30 crores in on plan side an~ 0.34 
crores on the non-plan side. The budgetary allocation during the last three years ranged from 
LO to 1.5 crores (plan as well as non-plan) and it was largely over-spent. The Committee 
observes that there is a considerable scope for enhancing the budgetary support under this 
head for stopping rabies in the country, for providing rearing homes for cows, for health care 
and sterilisation of animals and for prevention of cruelty to animals. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the budgetary support in respect of Animal Welfare Board needs 
to be considerably enhanced to say, Rs. 10 crores, for catering to the needs of the animals. At 
the same time , Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry to ensure that the 
enhanced budgetary support, if provided, are spent really for the benefit of the animals and 
not on illusory overheads . 
76. Central Zoo Authority incurred an expenditure of Rs. 3 crores equal to the amount 
provided as budgetary support. The budgetary provision in 1993-94 and 1994-95 ranged from 
Rs. 1.5 crore to Rs. 3 crores and it was over-spent . A budgetary provision of Rs. 3 crores has 
been made in the budget estimates for 1996-97 also. The Committee observes that the 
budgetary support is not spent Jor the purpose for which it is intended otherwise the death 

rate of 15 to 20 per cent of animals due to gastroenteritis in Indian zoos would not have been 
there. The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that the animals should be 
protected from heatstroke. They should be provided with good food and safe drinking water 
so that the death of animals on these counts are avoided. Steps should also be taken to 
provide a trained cadre of officers for management of zoos. The Committee is constrained to 
observe that a sum of Rs. 3 crores spent on evaluation of zoos was not properly spent as 
nothing appears to have been spent for rehabilitation purposes. In Committee's view there is a 
strong case for enhancing the budgetary allocation, say, Rs. 10 crores for Central Zoo 
Authority to say Rs. 10 crores so that the programmes relating to the welfare of the animals 
as also the creation of a cadre comprising of trained officers can be taken care of. 
77. A provision of Rs. 106 crores has been made in the budget estimates for 1996-97 in 
respect of Ganga Project Directorate. The main objective of GAP Phase-! is to improve the 
water quality of river Ganga. To that end, sewage generated from 25 class I towns 
(populations above 1 lakh) in U.P., Bihar, and the West Bengal is intercepted, diverted and 
treated before its final disposal either back in the river or for irrigation purposes. 261 
schemes of pollution abatement have been sanctioned which include interception and diversion 
of sewage, sewage treatment plants, low cost toilets, electric crematoria and bathing ghats, in 
the States of U.P., Bihar and the West Bengal. The action plan envisages diversion and 
treatment of 873 million litres per day of sewage from the above towns. Out of this, a capacity 
of 654 million Jitres per day has already been created. 
It has been stated that 244 schemes have been completed, the remaining 17 are in 
progress and expected to be completed by 31.03.1997. Of the 35 sewage treatment plants 
proposed to be constructed, 26 are functional and remaining 9 are in their final stages of 
completion. The project has tieen delayed due to reasons such as inexperience in the kind of 
work required, inordinate delays in land acquisition for certain schemes, litigation and court 
cases in Kanpur, Allahabad in U.P. and in West Bengal encroachment of sites of major 
projects in Calcutta and Patna, tendering and retendering of certain schemes due to 
contractual problems, delay in the external aid component of ·Kanpur and Mirzapur and 
diversion of funds by State Governments of U..P. and Bihar and consequent delayed release of 
the Central funding to the States for implementation of certain programmes. 
78. The Committee has been informed that the Ganga Action Plan Model with necessary 
corrections on the basis of lessons learnt and experience gained has been applied to all the 
major rivers of the country un,der the two schemes of GAP Phase-11 and the NRCP. It would 
take- about 10 years of time to complete these works. 
79. The Committee notes that a sum of Rs. 18.70 crores was surrendered against GAP 
Phase-1 and Rs. 70 crores in GAP Phase-11 Rs. 14 crores on NRCP and Rs. 3.30 crores on 
establishment. The Committee expresses its concern on the non-utilised component of the 
Ganga Action Plan. The Committee observes that non-utilisation/surrender of funds at least 
on some programmes could have been visualised and corrections made accordingly. Further, 
the Committee would like to be apprised of the mechanism put in place to monitor the 
working of various plants set up under the GAP, Phase-1 and whether any provision was 
incorporated in the contracts with contractors for liquidated damages for failure/delay in 
execution of contracts. 
80. On the basis of the oral evidence tendered before the Committee and the written 
submissions made, the Committee has regretfully come to the conclusion that the functioning 
of the Ministry of EnYironment and Forests is far from satisfactory. The Committee had 
asked for detailed and comprehensive notes on some of the issues like modern fire-fighting 

controls including helicopters and aircrafts, the Project Elephant and Ganga Action Plan and 
certain other issues. While notes have been supplied but those are not very detailed and lack 
critical analysis. For example, note on Project Elephant had no details on the issues the 
Committee had specifically asked for. The Committee had also asked for details of the 
indigenous species of plants planted and how bad they been received by the local people? 
Similarly, no details of the equipment etc. supplied under this project have been furnished. 
81. A large amount of expenditure of the Ministry is by way of grants-in-aid to the 
various State Governments and Non-Government Organisation (NGOs). It therefore becomes 
incumbent on the part of the Ministry to interact more closely with the grantee states and 
NGOs to ensure that the grants made available are in fact used for the purpose for which 
these are being made available. The Committee, however, feels that this part of the activity 
has not been taken seriously. In fact, whenever explanations and details were asked for during 
the course of oral evidence, the Committee was told that the same was under the State 
Government and the Ministry had no control over it. The Committee is unable to accept this 
explanation and recommends greater monitoring on the funds made available to different 
State Governments and NGOs. 
82. The Committee has also noted the delays in completion of various civil works 
undertaken by the l\linistry. The Committee would like to emphasise the importance of their 
timely completion so as to avoid cost-overruns and delays in the projects. 
83. The attention of the Committee has also been drawn to some of the observations in 
respect of review of various projects, as have appeared in the Report of the Comptoller and 
Auditor General of India, for the year ended 31st March, 1993 (No. 6 of 1994). Some of these 
observations are reproduced below:-
Under 'National social forestry project', aided by World Bank and the United States 
Agency for classification resulting in non-reimbursement (Himachal Pradesh), excess purchase 
of polythene granules, non-transfer of plantation areas to gram panchayats (Rajasthan), non­
compliance with orders resulting in loss of revenue, non-conformity to norms of World Bank 
resulting in non-reimbursement and excess procurement of vehicles (Uttar Pradesh) were 
notices in audit. World Bank's assessment of project weaknesses in Uttar · Pradesh indicated 
lack of marketing information system, problems in supply of seedlings, ineffective monitoring 
and analysis of project research . and its use in project management decisions. 
There were dalays in completion of Ganga Action Plan (GAP) programme in the 
'Integrated sanitation works in Kanpur and 1\·lirzapur'. Effective performance of the upflow 
anaerobic sludge blanket system is dependent upon the adoption of technology for chromium 
recovery from tanneries' discharges. A mid-term evaluation report (February · 1992) revealed 
that only 26 out of 151 tanneries were likely to adopt chromium recovery thereby affecting the 
performance of upflow anaerobic sludge blanket system. The technology for post-treatment of 
effluents from upflow anaerobic sludge blanket system was still in an experimental stage in 
Netherlands and therefore could not be adopted in India. 
Non-installation of equipments, training details not being available, delays in planning, detailed 
review not having been conducted were somt of the problems that affiicted the project: in respect of 
'Technical assistance and equipments' aided by Unitt>d Kingdom no details of the aid received were 
available. 
Aid provided by Governm'ent of Sweden for 'Strengthening of Indian Institute of Forest 
Management' could not be utilised substantively because of management problems, infighting in the 
faculty, problems in design of management development programmes etc. 
The project progress review report in its analysis also indicated lack of clarity in planning, 

problems in management and co-ordination by Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and problems 
in co-ordination between Indian Authorities and German Technical Co-operation Agency (GTZ) head 
office. No details of the aid received were available. 
Similar observations have appeared in respect of review covering the implementation of Schemes of 
Ganga Action Plan Phase-1 and an appraisal of its achievements at selected cities of Uttar Pradesh 
(U.P.), Bihar and West Bengal (W.B.) and Forest Survey of India (F.S.I.) as have appeared ln the 
Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, for the year ended 31st March, 1994 (No. 6 
of 1995). These are only a few of the observations. The list is endless. 
84. The Committee observes that these observations should be implemented expeditiously. The 
Committee would also take the opportunity to emphasise that foreign aid lo any form should be 
avoided where in all such cases the indigenous resources can be utilised.

1 
 
REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change  deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the contained in its „Three 
Hundred Sixty Second Report‟ on „Demands for Grants (2022-23) of the Department of Space‟.  The 
Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 15th March, 2022. 
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from Department of Space in respect of all 
the fifteen recommendations/observations contained in the „Three Hundred Sixty  Second Report ‟. 
The replies of the Department of Space have been categorized as follows:- 
Chapter I:        Recommendations/Observations which have been accept ed by the 
Government:  
Para Nos.:- 2.7, 2.8, 2.10, 3.3, 3.4, 4.3, 6.3, 7.3, 7.4, 8.3, 9.1, 9.2 and 9.3  
 Total recommendations – 13 accepted. 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Department has accepted its  thirteen 
recommendations/observations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report.  
Chapter II:       Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies:  
Para Nos.:- 2.4 and 5.3  
Total recommendations – 02 Not to be pursued further. 
The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Department 
and, therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations further. 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee: ‘Nil’ 
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: ‘Nil’ 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding chapters.  
 
  

2 
 
CHAPTER - I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021 -22 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FIANANCIAL YEAR 2022-23 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.1 The Committee makes note of the roadmap prepared by the Department for the year       
2022-23 with a hope that the Department would strive hard to ensure that the targets set for the 
year 2022 -23 are achieved and the budgetary support provided to the Department would be 
sufficient to sustain its major projects/schemes/programmes without any difficulty. 
(Para 2.7 of the 362nd Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2 The observations of the Committee are noted.   
Recommendations/Observations 
1.3 The Committee while scrutinising the targets set and progress achieved by the Department 
during the year 2021-22, observes that the Department had set the target of realisation and launch 
of Geo -Imaging Satellite (GISAT) for agriculture and disaster management applications which 
could not be achieved as the launch could not succeed. Likewise, the launch of India's first solar 
observatory Spacecraft, Aditya -L1, on-board PSLV was envisaged during the year 2021 -22 which 
has now been targeted during 2022 -23.  The Committee further notes that the Department had a 
plan to launch the 3rd generation Oceanographic satellite - Oceansat-3 on-board PSLV in the year 
2021-22 which has now been rescheduled to 2022 -23. The Committee, theref ore, recommends that 
the Department should strive hard to ensure that the newly set timeline for these components are 
honoured and further delay should not happen.                                                             (Para 2.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.4 The recommendations of the Committee regarding launch of Aditya -L1 and Oceansat-3 are 
noted.  The Department will take necessary steps to ensure the timely launch of these satellites. 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.5 The Committee hopes that the recruitment drives as intended by the Department would be 
completed in a time bound manner. The Committee also desires the Department to furnish its 
updated manpower status in the Action Taken Notes.                                                  (Para 2.10 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.6 Presently, the men -in-position at various DOS / ISRO Centres / Units is 16077 against the 
Sanctioned strength of 19610. The recruitment activities in DOS/ISRO were greatly affected by 
Covid-19 induced restrictions during last two years. Further, Department was in the process of 
carrying out detailed assessment of S&T manpower in ISRO, while factoring the impact of reforms. 
Based on this, necessary guidelines have been issued to initiate recruitment actions in campaign 
mode. 
 
 

3 
 
 
BUDGET ALLOCATION FOR CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES/PROJECTS 
SPACE TECHNOLOGY 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.7 The Committee hopes that the Department would make all out efforts to ensure full 
utilisation of the budgetary allocation for the year 2021 -22 during the remaining period of the 
financial year 2021-22.                                                                                                   (Para 3.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.8 At the end of the Financial Year 2021 -22, the actual expenditure of the Department under 
the head “Space Technology” was Rs.8873.63 crore with an utilisation factor of 99.34 % of RE 
allocations. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.9 The Committee further feels that the utilisation by the Department under various 
components such as Trisonic Wind Tunnel Facility Project (TWT); Small Satellite Launch Vehicle 
(SSLV); Launch pad for SSLV; Network for Space Object Tracking & Analysis (NETRA); Geo -
Imaging Satellite (GISAT); Resourcesat -3S & 3SA; Development of Space Mate rials & 
Components; Development & Supply of Aluminium alloy tankages (Pre -investment); and Capacity 
Building Programme (CBP) could have been better. The Committee, accordingly, desires the 
Department to revisit its fund utilisation strategy under these com ponents and take necessary 
remedial actions so that funds made available for them are utilised fully.                    (Para 3.4 ibid) 
Action Taken

RE allocations provided under Trisonic Wind Tunnel Facility Project (TWT); Small Satellite

Recommendations/Observations 
1.12 The Committee finds the overall financial performance of the Department under its 'Space

GENERAL OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.23 The Committee notes that the Department of Space has been making efforts in mapping the 
glacial lakes which span over more than 2.5 hectare in size and the said exercise has been 
completed in respect of the Ganga basin and Sutlej river and the data has already been complied in 
the atlas form. The Committee is of the view that it will be of great importance if an inventory about 
the glacier and glacial lakes in the Himalayan region is documented on yearly basis. This is crucial 
in light of many studies suggesting that there has been rapid increase in the number of glacial lakes 
due to retreat in the glaciers caused by the impact of g lobal warming and keeping into 
consideration the possible large scale flooding and destruction that could happen in future.  
Therefore, role of the Department, in the matter becomes all the more pivotal and significant in 
light of the fact that many such gl aciers are physically inaccessible for ground reporting. The 
Committee also feels that with the modern technology and better resolution satellite imagery the 
task of glacier lakes outburst monitoring can be done in a more scientific and robust manner. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to initiate action in this regard in a time bound 
manner and to make best use of its remote sensing services for the purpose. Adequate budgetary 
allocations should also be made for the same.                                                               (Para 9.1 ibid)  
 
 
 
 

8 
 
Action Taken 
1.24   i. As an implementing agency under the National Hydrology Project (NHP) of M inistry of 
Jal Shakti, National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)/ ISRO mapped Glacial lakes of size 
greater than 0.25  ha in Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river basins of Himalaya 
(including transboundary catchment flowing into Indian region), along with associated 
characteristics describing geometry, hydrology, topographic, etc., using Resourcesat -2 
LISS4 MX data. 28,043 such lakes have been mapped across these basins, and 
corresponding atlases have been published. Mapping and attribute assignment of  these 
Glacial lakes took nearly 3 years. 
 ii.  
(a) Glacial lake formation is a slow process and generally extends over long duration, 
except in cases like landslide dammed lakes. Considering the dynamicity of the 
glacial lakes and availability of usable (due to issues such as cloud, snow cover, 
shadow etc.) high resolution satellite data, it is desirable to ha ve Glacial lake 
inventory updation at periodicity around 3-5 years. 
Periodic updation of Glacial lake database can be taken up by the following 
Organisations: 
o Central Water Commission/NWIC 
o State Disaster Organisations/State Remote Sensing Centres 
NRSC/ ISR O would build capacity for the concerned Organisations and extend 
technical handholding. 
(b) In case of Glaciers, the dynamism (changes in glacier surface area; volume etc.) may 
not be perceivable on an annual basis, even on high resolution satellite data. Mos t of 
the Himalayan glaciers are covered with rock debris partially in their ablation zones 
which makes it difficult to monitor the changes in ice surface area of glaciers. 
Glacier mapping is practically done by visual interpretation, which would take more 
than a year for covering the entire Himalaya, using High resolution satellite data.   
Also, usable (cloud/snow -free) high resolution satellite data for the entire Himalaya 
may not be available every year.  
Monitoring of Glacier mass balance can also be done using geodetic methods such as 
DEM differencing. This has been done by many foreign researchers, which has 
established thinning of glaciers in the Himalaya. These assessments have been done 
for decadal or coarser time intervals.  
Glacier inventory and ch ange assessment have been done by Space Applications 
Center (SAC)/ ISRO over different time periods in the Himalaya (Annexure-I). 
Based on these experiences and scientific knowledge, it is proposed that inventory of 
Glaciers in the Indian Himalayan regions  would be required at time intervals of 10 -
15 years. This could be taken up by SAC/ ISRO, on demand from the concerned 
Ministry/ Department; such as Ministry of  Environment, Forests and Climate 
Change, Ministry of Jal Shakti etc.   
 
 
 

9 
 
iii. 
(a) Glacial Lake Monitoring by Central Water Commission (CWC)/NWIC 
o Central Water Commission (CWC) is mandated by Government of India to provide 
Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) early warning. 
o NRSC/ ISRO imparted necessary training & technical handholding to Morphology & 
Climate Change Directorate, Central Water Commission, during 2015 for monitoring 
of glacial lakes using satellite data. Morphology & Climate Change Directorate, 
CWC is internally carrying out the monitoring Glacial lakes (>50ha) using satellite 
data since 2016 and monthly reports are web published 
(http://www.cwc.gov.in/glacial-lakeswater-bodies-himalayan-region). 
o NRSC/ISRO further conducted one -week training to CWC Officials in 2021 on 
“Monitoring of Glacial Lakes using Satellite Remote Sensing Data. Updat ed Glacial 
lake data base (size GT 0.25a) prepared by NRSC/ ISRO under NHP is also shared 
with CWC for use in monitoring of glacial lakes. 
o Hence, it is suggested that CWC may continue to monitor glacial lakes using updated 
glacial lake database provided by NRSC/ ISRO. 
(b) Glacial Lake Monitoring by State Organisations /State Remote Sensing Centres 
o State Government Departments located in Himalayan region can monitor glacial 
lakes concerned to their geographical region on regular basis for better and efficient 
management of glacial lake floods.  
o NRSC/ ISRO can build capacity and extend technical handholding for the concerned 
State Organisations on monitoring of glacial lakes using satellite data. 
o It is also informed that the Power Organisations such as NHPC, SJVNL , etc. are also 
gearing up for periodic monitoring of Glacial lakes using satellite data 
(c) GLOF studies at ISRO 
Glacial lake outburst flood modelling of prioritised glacial lakes are being done by 
NRSC/ ISRO, under NHP. 
Further, SAC/ISRO would carry out rese arch on developing method to identify potential 
areas around the lakes which could create temporary damming, and could lead to GLOFs.

Annexure-I 
Glacier inventory was carried out by SAC/ISRO over Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins 
using IRS P6  satellite data of (AWiFS and LISS -III sensor) for the periods; 2004 -2007 and 2007 -
2010. During Phase-I of the project, inventory was generated for all the glaciers in the Indus, Ganga 
and the Brahmaputra basins encompassing the Himalayas, Trans -Himalaya and Karakoram regions 
on 1: 50,000 scale using Resourcesat -1 satellite data of 2004 –2007 period. The results show that 
there are 32, 392 glaciers covering 71,182 sq. km area in the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins 
draining into the Indian territory. Duri ng Phase-II, the work was extended to map glaciers of West 
Indus basin which are draining into neighbouring countries. Thus the total glacier inventory data for 
all the three Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins show that there are 34919 glaciers covering 7 5, 
779 sq. km area. An updation of the Glaciers‟ inventory is proposed systematically; selectively over 
Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins with the help of collaborating agencies in respective states 
with recent satellite images. 
Glacier monitoring has be en carried out for select Glaciers using satellite data at SAC/ 
ISRO, which may represent the general trend of the Glacier dynamics. Changes in area of glaciers 
for the time period of 1962 – 2001/04/05 were mapped for 2630 glaciers. Glacier extents for 196 2 
were taken from Survey of India (SOI) topographical maps on 1:50,000 scale as reference and that 
of 2001/04/05 timeframe were taken from satellite data. This study showed a total loss of 13.4 % in 
area of glaciers. In continuation, monitoring of change i n extents of 2018 glaciers was carried out 
from IRS LISS III data of year 2000/01/02 and 2010/2011. The monitoring showed that 87% of the 
glaciers had no change, 12% have retreated and 1 % glaciers have advanced. This gives a net loss of 
20.94 sq. km in th e total area of 10,250.68 sq. km for all the monitored glaciers mapped in the year 
2000/01. Net change in glaciated area varies from region to region.  
Further, 5234 glaciers were monitored between the years 2001 and 2017/2018 across 
Himalayan –Karakoram ( H-K) region from Kashmir to Sikkim using IRS LISS III and limited 
Landsat data. These 5234 ice bodies included 3435 debris free glaciers also. In Karakoram region 
(north of Indus river), 2058 glacier bodies were checked and mapped. In this region, gain in area 
(0.056 %) has been observed in the area coverage of 17902.95 Km 2. The loss observed in rest of 
Himalayan region varies from 0.751 % for sub -basins south of Indus river (or in rest of Jammu and 
Kashmir and Ladakh states), 2.32 % in Himachal Pradesh or in Chenab and Sutlej basins, 0.84 % in 
Uttarakhand, 2.164 % in parts of Nepal, and 2.147 % in Sikkim or Tista sub -basin. SAC/ ISRO has 
taken up glacier monitoring using recent satellite images.
